title: The veneration of Rod Liddle shows the emptiness of modern conservatism
gist: Following columnist Rod Liddle's death, the Spectator's lavish tributes compared him to Jonathan Swift, but the author argues that unlike Swift — whose satire enacted real political change — Liddle's writing only reinforced his readers' existing prejudices, and that the scale of his veneration by senior Conservatives exposes the emptiness of a party that now defines itself purely by what it opposes.

insights.claim: After Spectator columnist Rod Liddle died aged 66 on 2nd August, the magazine put its homepage and cover in black and devoted much of its next issue to tributes from former editors Boris Johnson and Fraser Nelson, current editor Michael Gove, Toby Young, Douglas Murray and former Spectator digital head Kemi Badenoch.
insights.speaker: Peter Williams
insights.so_what: Establishes the scale and seniority of the tributes that the article goes on to critique.
insights.quote: After decking out its homepage in black, the grand old magazine devoted the cover (masthead also in black) and much of the inside of its next issue to Liddle
insights.locator: Let no one accuse the Spectator

insights.claim: Boris Johnson eulogised Liddle as 'the last gunslinger in town, blazing away from his lonely but glorious redoubt', while Michael Gove compared Liddle's time at the BBC to seeing 'Jack Sparrow at Henley regatta' and said he 'knew he had to puncture it with a broadsword'.
insights.speaker: Peter Williams
insights.so_what: Captures the tone of the tributes — 'amusingly macho' framing of Liddle as a fearless outsider — that the author will go on to dismantle.
insights.quote: To Johnson, Liddle was the last gunslinger in town, “blazing away from his lonely but glorious redoubt”.
insights.locator: Much of the lionisation of their fearless free-speech warrior

insights.claim: Fraser Nelson declared Liddle 'the greatest satirist since Swift', a comparison Michael Gove endorsed and extended by also invoking George Orwell.
insights.speaker: Peter Williams
insights.so_what: Sets up the central comparison the article uses to evaluate whether the veneration of Liddle was deserved.
insights.quote: After Fraser Nelson declared him “the greatest satirist since Swift”, Gove ran with the comparison, also invoking George Orwell.

insights.claim: Andrew Gilligan, who worked under Liddle at the Today programme, said Liddle's 'only real mission was épater la bourgeoisie' — to provoke liberal and left-leaning critics on behalf of his targets, who included women, Muslims, gay people, Afro-Caribbean youths and schoolchildren.
insights.speaker: Andrew Gilligan
insights.so_what: Offers a more critical insider assessment of Liddle's actual professional purpose, distinct from the eulogies' framing.
insights.quote: His only real mission was épater la bourgeoisie

insights.claim: The author argues the Swift comparison is 'bait worth taking' not because it is absurd, but because examining it reveals the true, most important target of Liddle's writing: his own readers.
insights.speaker: Peter Williams
insights.so_what: States the article's analytical hinge: the comparison is used as a tool to expose what Liddle's columns were really doing.
insights.quote: But the Swift comparison is bait worth taking, not because it is egregious but because of what it says about the third, and most important, target of Liddle’s writing, his readers.
insights.locator: But the Swift comparison is bait worth taking

insights.claim: Unlike most satirists, who become a branch of the establishment despite their mockery, Jonathan Swift produced real political change: while working for Robert Harley's Tory ministry, his pamphlet 'The Conduct of the Allies' helped turn public opinion against the War of the Spanish Succession, and his Drapier's Letters, written while exiled in Dublin, stirred the Irish public against a scheme that would have flooded their economy with debased coinage.
insights.speaker: Peter Williams
insights.so_what: Provides the concrete historical evidence for why Swift is considered a genuine agent of political change, the standard against which Liddle is being measured.
insights.quote: his pamphlet “The Conduct of the Allies” helped turn opinion against the war of the Spanish succession. Once he was exiled in Dublin, his Drapier’s Letters stirred the Irish public against a scheme that would have flooded their economy with debased coinage.
insights.locator: This was not true of Swift

insights.claim: Swift's ultimate goal, as expressed in a letter to Alexander Pope while writing Gulliver's Travels, was to change his readers' fundamental worldview — disproving the definition of man as a rational animal — and he wrote that he would 'never have peace of mind till all honest men are of my opinion.'
insights.speaker: Peter Williams
insights.so_what: Shows Swift's satire was explicitly designed to convert readers to a new perspective, not merely entertain existing ones.
insights.quote: Upon this great foundation of misanthropy, though not in Timon's manner, the whole building of my Travels is erected; and I never will have peace of mind till all honest men are of my opinion.
insights.locator: But more than that, his goal

themes.theme: What satire is supposed to do

insights.claim: The author argues that any substantial work of art enacts change, however modest, in how its audience sees the world — not necessarily in what they think, but in how they perceive it — and that comedy achieves this as well as any art form because a joke's punchline is itself a unit of change.
insights.speaker: Peter Williams
insights.so_what: Sets the standard the author uses to judge whether Liddle's work counts as real satire or something lesser.
insights.quote: Any substantial work of art will enact change, however modestly, in those who encounter it; not necessarily in what we think, but in how we see the world.

insights.claim: The apparent tolerance of unsparing mockery in British political culture, from medieval court fools through Gillray and Beyond the Fringe, is actually good for those in power, since it stands as proof no revolution is needed — and it limits satirists, who become part of the establishment rather than authentic outsiders.
insights.speaker: Peter Williams
insights.so_what: Argues Britain's satire tradition is fundamentally non-threatening to power, complicating the 'fearless outsider' framing applied to Liddle.
insights.quote: The apparent tolerance of unsparing mockery and exposure is good for those in power, who can stand it as proof that we have no need for revolutions. And it is a limitation for satirists, who are apt to become a branch of the establishment, however ersatz, rather than authentic outsiders.
insights.locator: Satire, which most people take to mean

insights.claim: The author says British satirists from Peter Cook and Private Eye to Rory Bremner and Yes, Minister ultimately amount to one set of public-school-educated comparatively bohemian figures 'flicking elastic bands' at the preppier types who become head boy.
insights.speaker: Peter Williams
insights.so_what: Frames the entire British satirical establishment, not just Liddle, as class-insular and ultimately unthreatening to the powerful.
insights.quote: one never escapes the sense of one set of public-school boys—comparatively bohemian, but public-school boys nonetheless—flicking elastic bands across the common room at the preppier types who become head boy
insights.locator: From Peter Cook and Private Eye

insights.claim: Musical satirist Tom Lehrer observed of his own songs that satire is 'not even preaching to the converted; it's titillating the converted' — a description the author says applies equally to Rod Liddle.
insights.speaker: Tom Lehrer
insights.so_what: Provides a memorable, third-party formulation of the article's central critique of satire's limited real-world effect.
insights.quote: As Tom Lehrer remarked of his own satirical songs, “It’s not even preaching to the converted; it’s titillating the converted”, and that applies whether it’s Stewart Lee on Ukip, James Acaster on Ricky Gervais, or Liddle himself.

themes.theme: Liddle's real function: reassurance, not change

insights.claim: Rod Liddle's job, the author argues, 'was nothing more radical than tickling his readers' bellies' — he cultivated an in-group through excoriation of out-groups, reinforcing rather than altering his readers' pre-existing worldview.
insights.speaker: Peter Williams
insights.so_what: This is the article's central verdict on Liddle's actual craft, distinguishing him sharply from the transformative satire of Swift.
insights.quote: Liddle’s job, by contrast, was nothing more radical than tickling his readers’ bellies. Like most columnists and comedians, he cultivated an in-group via excoriation of out-groups.

insights.claim: Liddle's purpose was to reassure readers that, whatever their foibles and prejudices, they stood on the side of common sense and humanity, while flattering their own sense of liberality as they watched him demolish other people's sacred cows.
insights.speaker: Peter Williams
insights.so_what: Specifies the psychological mechanism by which Liddle's columns worked on his readership, per the author.
insights.quote: His purpose was not to alter his readers’ worldview but reinforce it, to reassure them that, whatever their foibles and prejudices, they stood on the side of common sense and humanity, while also giving them a flattering sense of their own liberality as they watched him demolish other people’s sacred cows.
insights.locator: His purpose was not to alter

insights.claim: The author judges that to compare Liddle to Swift or writers of similar stature 'is to mistake a hack for an artist'.
insights.speaker: Peter Williams
insights.so_what: Delivers the article's sharpest single verdict on Liddle's literary standing relative to the comparison made in his tributes.
insights.quote: To compare him to Swift and writers of like stature is to mistake a hack for an artist.
insights.locator: He also had some points to make

insights.claim: The author argues the excessive veneration of Liddle is itself an indictment of the modern Conservative party, which he describes as 'an empty vessel led by an empty vessel' that defines itself by what it opposes — not woke, not net zero, not in the EU, and now not in the ECHR either.
insights.speaker: Peter Williams
insights.so_what: Extends the critique of Liddle into a broader political thesis about the current state of British conservatism.
insights.quote: The excessive veneration is also an indictment of the modern Conservative party: an empty vessel led by an empty vessel; a movement that defines itself by what it is not. Not woke. Not net zero. Not in the EU and, now that that great benison has been secured, not in the ECHR either.

insights.claim: The author cites Kemi Badenoch's new adviser on combating extremism, former neo-Nazi Joshua Bonehill-Paine, as being connected to the faux-satirical AI-generated content produced by the YouTube channel the Crewkerne Gazette, which the author describes as low-quality material lacking any real satirical value.
insights.speaker: Peter Williams
insights.so_what: Extends the critique of empty, low-value 'satire' from Liddle to the current Conservative leadership's associates.
insights.quote: One of his lesser-remarked offences is being handmaiden to the faux-satirical AI slop excreted by the YouTube channel the Crewkerne Gazette.
